**Mary: A Fiction** by Mary Wollstonecraft is a deeply philosophical and emotional novel that explores the life of its titular character, Mary, as she navigates through a series of trials and tribulations. The story is a poignant reflection on themes such as love, loss, sensibility, and the societal constraints placed on women during the late 18th century.

Mary, the protagonist, is portrayed as a woman of strong intellect and deep emotions, whose life is shaped by her relationships and her internal struggles. The novel begins with Mary's upbringing in a family that values material wealth over emotional well-being, leading to her isolation and quest for meaning. Her marriage, arranged for financial reasons, proves loveless and further isolates her. The death of her friend Ann and her subsequent travels to Lisbon add layers of sorrow and introspection to her character.

Throughout the novel, Wollstonecraft delves into Mary's internal world, highlighting her sensitivity, her capacity for love, and her struggle to reconcile her desires with the societal expectations placed upon her. The novel's exploration of Mary's emotional depth and her interactions with other characters, particularly Henry, serves to underscore the limitations and challenges faced by women in her position.

The narrative is notable for its rich, descriptive language and its focus on the inner life of the protagonist, which was a departure from the more structured and societal-focused novels of the time. Wollstonecraft's portrayal of Mary's emotional struggles and her ultimate resignation to her fate offers a powerful commentary on the human condition and the resilience of the spirit in the face of adversity.

Overall, *Mary: A Fiction* is a significant work that not only showcases Wollstonecraft's literary skill but also provides insight into the experiences of women in the 18th century, making it a compelling read for those interested in feminist literature and the history of the novel.

this supports me.

great affliction; but I am not alone--I have my God, who is my refuge,
and will be my strength. I have not a wish unblighted; but if any, it
is to be united to those who have gone before me. I am still a wanderer,
but not without a resting-place in view. I will labour to walk in the
path he trod--to be as pure and good as he was. This is my only
consolation.

other parts of the Scripture, particularly the Proverbs, in which he has
marked some passages with his own hand. These have been my
companions--they have taught me to find fault with myself, and to be
satisfied with my lot. The Proverbs have shown me how much I need
instruction. I have made a resolution to read them every day.

I have also found some of his notes; this is one: "Mary is the most
interesting object of my care; her happiness is intertwined with my
existence." Another: "To be loved by Mary, and to die, is to be happy."
Another: "She is a bright ornament of her sex--an exemplar of every
virtue; and as a legacy, I commit her to the care of that Being who
alone can make her happy." When I read these, my heart is pierced with
grief, but also filled with comfort. I have no words to express my
feelings.

I have a deep sense of my own unworthiness. I have no friend to advise
me; but I am resolved to follow the duties of my station, and to be
useful. I have a house, but it is not my home. The company of the
world is a burden; but I must not be a hindrance to others. I shall
endeavor to be cheerful, but my heart is heavy. I have no comforter. I
am in a desolate land. I know that my Redeemer liveth, but I am in
darkness.

I have only one request, that my dear mother would take me under her
protection. I have written to her; but fear she will refuse. I am
afraid--the thought is a heavy burden. I have no home. I am a wanderer

shepherd. I am lost.

But I will not complain. I will trust in the Lord, and do good. I have

will not murmur. I will not be discouraged. I will look to him for
strength. I will do what is right. I will be humble and patient.

guide. His loss is my constant grief. I feel it more deeply than I can
express. Yet I must not indulge in useless sorrow. I must not let it
overpower me. I will try to be strong. I will try to resign myself to the
will of God.

woman, with no one to help me. I fear I shall fall. I fear I shall give
way to my grief. But I will not, I must not. I will trust in God. I will
pray for strength. I will read his word. I will seek comfort in him.

do better. I will seek to be more like my Henry. I will follow his

Mary, the protagonist, is the daughter of Edward and Eliza. Her mother is described as fashionable but indolent, with a focus on appearances rather than substance. Mary's early life is marked by neglect, left to her own devices, developing a vivid imagination and a sensitive nature. She spends her time reading and exploring nature, forming a deep connection with the natural world and the idea of a divine presence.

**CHAPTER II**

Mary grows up in a neglectful environment, with her mother more focused on superficialities than her children. Mary's siblings die young, and she is left to care for her ailing mother. Despite the neglect, Mary develops a strong sense of compassion and moral responsibility. She befriends Ann, a young woman from a poor family, and they share a deep bond. Mary's intellectual curiosity leads her to read widely, developing her thinking abilities.

**CHAPTER III**

Ann's family faces financial ruin, and Mary tries to help them. Ann becomes infatuated with a man who later disappoints her, leading to her decline. **CHAPTER IV**

Mary explores the natural beauty around her, finding solace in the grandeur of the mountains, rivers, and the sea. She contemplates the divine and develops a sense of devotion. Her intellectual pursuits and emotional depth set her apart, making her a singular character.

**CHAPTER V**

Mary's brother dies, making her an heiress. Her mother begins to take notice of her, but Mary is more concerned about Ann's well-being. The family's financial dispute leads to a potential marriage arrangement for Mary. She is forced into a hasty marriage to secure the estate, which she accepts reluctantly, prioritizing Ann's needs over her own happiness.

**CHAPTER VI**

After her mother's death, Mary's husband leaves for the continent. She focuses on Ann, whose health deteriorates. Mary's marriage becomes a source of dread, and she seeks solace in her friendship with Ann. Despite her efforts, Ann's health worsens, leading to her death, which devastates Mary.

**CHAPTER VII**

Mary's father dies, and she is left to care for her friend Ann, whose health is failing. Ann's death leaves Mary in a state of despair. She decides to leave Lisbon, seeking solace in new surroundings. Her journey is marked by emotional turmoil and a deep sense of loss.

**CHAPTER VIII**

Mary travels to Lisbon with Ann, hoping the change of air will help her friend. Despite initial hopes, Ann's health declines further. Mary's emotional state is fragile, and she finds comfort in the presence of Henry, a kind and thoughtful man she meets. Their bond grows, but Mary's internal conflict between her duty to her husband and her feelings for Henry intensifies.

**CHAPTER IX**

Mary and Henry's relationship deepens, but they face societal pressures and personal constraints. Henry's health declines, and Mary's emotional struggles continue. She grapples with her feelings, torn between her duty and her heart.

**CHAPTER X**

Mary's internal conflict reaches a peak as she prepares to leave Lisbon. Henry's illness worsens, and she is torn between caring for him and her duty to her husband. The chapter highlights her emotional turmoil and the societal expectations that constrain her.

**CHAPTER XI**

Mary returns to England, where she faces the harsh realities of poverty and societal ills. She tries to help the poor but is met with ingratitude, deepening her despair. Her reflections on sensibility and virtue are central to her character development.

**CHAPTER XII**

Mary's health declines, and she becomes increasingly isolated. She finds solace in her faith and the memory of Henry. Her letters reveal her deep emotional pain and her struggle to find meaning in a world that seems hostile.

**CHAPTER XIII**

Mary's story concludes with her death, three months after Henry's passing. Her letter to her mother expresses her resignation to her fate, her faith in God, and her resolve to follow the path of virtue. The novel ends with a sense of tragic inevitability, underscoring the societal constraints and personal sorrows that shaped her life.

consoler of others; but for the present, she was a living monument of

The novel *Mary* by Mary Wollstonecraft is a deeply personal and philosophical exploration of a young woman's life, marked by intense emotions, intellectual curiosity, and a struggle with societal expectations. The story follows Mary, the protagonist, through her formative years, her relationships, and her internal conflicts, ultimately leading to her tragic demise.

### Plot Summary:
1. **Childhood and Family Dynamics**: Mary grows up in a household where her parents are emotionally distant and focused on material comfort. Her father is tyrannical, and her mother is indifferent, leaving Mary to seek comfort in nature, books, and her own imagination.

2. **Friendship and Intellectual Growth**: Mary forms a deep bond with Ann, a neighbor, which becomes a central part of her life. She also develops a passion for reading and intellectual pursuits, which sets her apart from her family.

3. **Marriage and Loss**: Mary is forced into a marriage with Charles, which she deeply resents. Her life becomes one of isolation and sorrow, exacerbated by the death of her friend Ann and her own failing health.

4. **Journey and Reflection**: Seeking solace, Mary travels to Lisbon with Ann, where she meets Henry, a kind and intellectual man who offers her emotional support. Despite her growing feelings for Henry, Mary's health declines, and she faces a series of tragic events, including Ann's death and Henry's terminal illness.

5. **Tragic Conclusion**: Henry's death leaves Mary devastated. She struggles with grief and the societal pressures that restrict her. In the end, Mary's sensibility and emotional depth lead to her own demise, as she cannot reconcile her internal turmoil with the harsh realities of her world.

### Themes:
- **Sensibility and Emotion**: The novel emphasizes Mary's intense emotional life, highlighting both the beauty and the pain that come from deep feeling.
- **Feminism and Society**: Wollstonecraft critiques the societal constraints placed on women, particularly in education and marriage, reflecting her broader feminist views.
- **Religion and Philosophy**: Mary's spiritual struggles and philosophical musings are central to the narrative, exploring themes of faith, morality, and the search for meaning.
- **Nature and Solitude**: Nature serves as both a refuge and a mirror for Mary's internal state, underscoring her connection to the natural world.

### Style and Significance:
Wollstonecraft's writing is characterized by its lyrical prose, deep psychological insight, and exploration of themes that were radical for her time. *Mary* is a precursor to the feminist literature of the 19th century and remains a powerful exploration of individual struggle and societal critique.

Overall, *Mary* is a poignant and thought-provoking novel that delves into the complexities of the human spirit, offering a raw and unflinching look at the challenges faced by women in the late 18th century.

**Enoch Soames**

By Max Beerbohm

When a book about the literature of the eighteen-nineties was given to the world by Mr. Holbrook Jackson, I looked eagerly in the index for Soames, Enoch. It was as I feared: he was not there. But everybody else was. Many writers whom I had quite forgotten, or remembered but faintly, lived again for me, they and their work, in Mr. Holbrook Jackson's pages. The book was as thorough as it was brilliantly written. And thus the omission found by me was an all the deadlier record of poor Soames's failure to impress himself on his decade.

I dare say I am the only person who noticed the omission. Soames had failed so piteously as all that! Nor is there a counterpoise in the thought that if he had had some measure of success he might have passed, like those others, out of my mind, to return only at the historian's beck. It is true that had his gifts, such as they were, been acknowledged in his lifetime, he would never have made the bargain I saw him make--that strange bargain whose results have kept him always in the foreground of my memory. But it is from those very results that the full piteousness of him glares out.

Not my compassion, however, impels me to write of him. For his sake, poor fellow, I should be inclined to keep my pen out of the ink. It is ill to deride the dead. And how can I write about Enoch Soames without making him ridiculous? Or, rather, how am I to hush up the horrid fact that he WAS ridiculous? I shall not be able to do that. Yet, sooner or later, write about him I must. You will see in due course that I have no option. And I may as well get the thing done now.

In the summer term of '93 a bolt from the blue flashed down on Oxford. It drove deep; it hurtlingly embedded itself in the soil. Dons and undergraduates stood around, rather pale, discussing nothing but it. Whence came it, this meteorite? From Paris. Its name? Will Rothenstein. Its aim? To do a series of twenty-four portraits in lithograph. These were to be published from the Bodley Head, London. The matter was urgent. Already the warden of A, and the master of B, and the Regius Professor of C had meekly "sat." Dignified and doddering old men who had never consented to sit to any one could not withstand this dynamic little stranger. He did not sue; he invited: he did not invite; he commanded. He was twenty-one years old. He wore spectacles that flashed more than any other pair ever seen. He was a wit. He was brimful of ideas. He knew Whistler. He knew Daudet and the Goncourts. He knew every one in Paris. He knew them all by heart. He was Paris in Oxford. It was whispered that, so soon as he had polished off his selection of dons, he was going to include a few undergraduates. It was a proud day for me when I--I was included. I liked Rothenstein not less than I feared him; and there arose between us a friendship that has grown ever warmer, and been more and more valued by me, with every passing year.

At the end of term he settled in, or, rather, meteoritically into, London. It was to him I owed my first knowledge of that forever-enchanting little world-in-itself, Chelsea, and my first acquaintance with Walter Sickert and other August elders who dwelt there. It was Rothenstein that took me to see, in Cambridge Street, Pimlico, a young man whose drawings were already famous among the few--Aubrey Beardsley by name. With Rothenstein I paid my first visit to the Bodley Head. By him I was inducted into another haunt of intellect and daring, the domino-room of the Cafe Royal.

There, on that October evening--there, in that exuberant vista of gilding and crimson velvet set amidst all those opposing mirrors and upholding caryatids, with fumes of tobacco ever rising to the painted and pagan ceiling, and with the hum of presumably cynical conversation broken into so sharply now and again by the clatter of dominoes shuffled on marble tables, I drew a deep breath and, "This indeed," said I to myself, "is life!" (Forgive me that theory. Remember the waging of even the South African War was not yet.)

It was the hour before dinner. We drank vermuth. Those who knew Rothenstein were pointing him out to those who knew him only by name. Men were constantly coming in through the swing-doors and wandering slowly up and down in search of vacant tables or of tables occupied by friends. One of these rovers interested me because I was sure he wanted to catch Rothenstein's eye. He had twice passed our table, with a hesitating look; but Rothenstein, in the thick of a disquisition on Puvis de Chavannes, had not seen him. He was a stooping, shambling person, rather tall, very pale, with longish and brownish hair. He had a thin, vague beard, or, rather, he had a chin on which a large number of hairs weakly curled and clustered to cover its retreat. He was an odd-looking person; but in the nineties odd apparitions were more frequent, I think, than they are now. The young writers of that era--and I was sure this man was a writer--strove earnestly to be distinct in aspect. This man had striven unsuccessfully. He wore a soft black hat of clerical kind, but of Bohemian intention, and a gray waterproof cape which, perhaps because it was waterproof, failed to be romantic. I decided that "dim" was the mot juste for him. I had already essayed to write, and was immensely keen on the mot juste, that Holy Grail of the period.

The dim man was now again approaching our table, and this time he made up his mind to pause in front of it.

"You don't remember me," he said in a toneless voice.

Rothenstein brightly focused him.

"Yes, I do," he replied after a moment, with pride rather than effusion--pride in a retentive memory. "Edwin Soames."

"Enoch Soames," said Enoch.

"Enoch Soames," repeated Rothenstein in a tone implying that it was enough to have hit on the surname. "We met in Paris a few times when you were living there. We met at the Cafe Groche."

"And I came to your studio once."

"Oh, yes; I was sorry I was out."

"But you were in. You showed me some of your paintings, you know. I hear you're in Chelsea now."

"Yes."

I almost wondered that Mr. Soames did not, after this monosyllable, pass along. He stood patiently there, rather like a dumb animal, rather like a donkey looking over a gate. A sad figure, his. It occurred to me that "hungry" was perhaps the mot juste for him; but--hungry for what? He looked as if he had little appetite for anything. I was sorry for him; and Rothenstein, though he had not invited him to Chelsea, did ask him to sit down and have something to drink.

Seated, he was more self-assertive. He flung back the wings of his cape with a gesture which, had not those wings been waterproof, might have seemed to hurl defiance at things in general. And he ordered an absinthe. "Je me tiens toujours fidele," he told Rothenstein, "a la sorciere glauque."

"It is bad for you," said Rothenstein, dryly.

"Nothing is bad for one," answered Soames. "Dans ce monde il n'y a ni bien ni mal."

"Nothing good and nothing bad? How do you mean?"

"I explained it all in the preface to 'Negations.'"

"'Negations'?"

"Yes, I gave you a copy of it."

"Oh, yes, of course. But, did you explain, for instance, that there was no such thing as bad or good grammar?"

her. We talk a great deal about Boston and Paris, and we have a great
many things in common. She is very "emancipated," as they say here, and
thinks nothing of going about alone, or of doing anything she likes. I
must say she is a very interesting girl, though I can't help thinking she
is a little too much so. She has a way of saying things that is quite
startling sometimes, but it's very amusing. She tells me the most
interesting things about America, and I am always glad to see her.

As for the others here, I don't care so much for them. There is a young
man from Boston who is very well-read and very interesting in his way,
but he is rather too much like all the rest. He is so dreadfully
aesthetic that it is almost affected; but he is very kind, and very good
to me. And then there are two or three others that I don't care so much
about. I don't like the American girl from New York so much as I like
Miss Hope. She is very pretty and very fashionable, but she is so very
haughty and so hard to get on with. She doesn't seem to want to know me,
and when I have tried to talk to her, she has been very cold and
distant. She is what I call a _real_ American; I don't know what it is,
but they have such a different way. I don't think she likes me either;
but that is of no consequence. It is not very agreeable, but I can
endure it.

I must now close. I hope you will write to me when you have time, and
tell me all the news. I am very much in need of hearing from home. I am
very sorry to leave Paris, but I think I can make the best of it.

Yours, dear Lady Augusta,

Evelyn Vane.

In this way, I am afraid I shall not be able to come to you on the 7th;
but I do hope you will write to me at Hyeres, where I shall be staying.
You can't think how much I should look forward to getting a letter from
you; all your letters are so charming, so clever, so full of life. I
wish I had the gift of writing like you; but I have not a bit of talent,
dear Lady Augusta, and I can only tell you the simple things that happen
to me, in the simplest way.

I have been having a rather curious experience here, in this Parisian
boarding-house, where I am staying. It is such a strange, mixed society,
and so different from any I ever was in before. I am sure you would find
it most interesting. There are people of all kinds, from all countries,
and of all shades of opinion. The most curious of all is a young woman
from America--a Miss Miranda Hope, I think her name is. She is very
emancipated, and has some very strange ideas about the position of woman
and the rights of the sexes. She is a great friend of the French, and
thinks everything of their way of looking at life; she says they are the
only people who have any real appreciation for the beautiful. She is
constantly talking about the "position of woman," and seems to think that
if I were only more aggressive I should be happier. But I don't think
aggressiveness would make me happier, do you, dear Lady Augusta? I think
it would only make me very tired. She is very interesting, but she is not
at all like any one I have ever known before. Her appearance is very
singular--she is very tall and lean, and has a very peculiar way of
dressing. But that's a detail.

But then there is a young Mr. Leverett, an American, too, who is a great
friend of the beautiful; he is a sort of aesthetic Bostonian, and has a
great many beautiful ideas. He is very cultivated, but he is not very
robust; he seems to be suffering from the climate here, which is very
trying for delicate people. He is very enthusiastic about the French and
their way of looking at life, and he has told me a great deal about
Boston, which seems to be a very curious place. Then there is a German
gentleman, a professor, who is very learned, and has a great deal to say
about everything. He is very fond of discussion, and is constantly
arguing with the young American girl, who is very bold and
uncompromising.

The most curious thing is the mixture of nationalities here. The French
themselves are not very well represented, but the mistress of the house is
a very clever woman, who seems to manage everything in a most
admirable way. She is a very good talker, and has a great deal of
tact; but sometimes she seems to me rather hard, and I don't think she
likes the Americans very much. She is not too kind to her own daughters,
who are rather meagre and not very interesting. There is one son, who is
very polite, and who has been taking me out a good deal to see Paris. He
is very well mannered, and I think he has a great many pleasant qualities,
but he is not very sincere. I don't think he says what he really
thinks--he says a good many things that he must know are not true. But
that is perhaps the way of the French.

The English contingent is, as you may suppose, very small; but I have made
some acquaintance with a Mr. and Miss Westgate, who are here from London,
and who seem very nice. They are not very talkative, but they are very
kind and considerate. I have also seen a little of a very nice German
family, who have a most fascinating daughter, but she is not very
attractive. The men, in general, are not very agreeable. The Americans
are rather too much the opposite of the English; they are too
conspicuous, too loud, too pretentious. The women especially have a way
of talking as if they had authority on every subject, which is very
tiresome.

But the most tiresome thing of all is the "aesthetic" young man from
Boston. He is always talking about art and beauty, and is constantly
quoting French authors and artists. But, although he is very interesting
in a way, I feel that he is rather artificial and insincere. He has a
great deal of affectation, and I think he is not quite a real man. Still,
he is very agreeable to talk with, especially when he is discussing
pictures and other things of that sort. But I can't help thinking that he
is not a bit better than the others, in his own way. It is all rather
confusing, but I think I am getting a great deal of benefit from all
these new experiences. I must tell you more about all this when I see
you.

I must close now, as my letter is already very long, and I have so much to
do before I leave Paris. I do hope you can manage to come to Hyeres, but
I suppose it is a great deal to ask. Do write to me there, and let me
know that you have got this letter safely.

Yours ever,

Evelyn Vane.

- The trial of Jim Weston begins.

- It was first published in 1991, long after its creation in 1930, due to the personal and professional conflicts between the authors.

She appears not to notice what Asakawa has in her hands, as her gaze has already shifted to the sliding closet door. She regards it almost druggedly. RYOMI (haltingly) This... this is where Tomoko died. FLASHBACK RYOMI (O.S.) Tomoko! Ryomis hands fling aside the CLOSET DOOR. Within, she finds the pale blue CARCASS of her daughter, curled up into an unnatural fetal position. Tomokos mouth yawns gaping, her eyes glassy and rolled up into the back of her head. Her hands are caught in her hair, as if trying to pull it out by the roots. It is a horrific scene, one that says Tomoko died as if from some unspeakable fear. PRESENT Ryomi sinks to her knees, hitting the wooden floor hard. She puts her face into her hands and begins sobbing loudly. Asakawa says nothing. EXT. ASAKAWAS APARTMENT KITCHEN - DAY Asakawa wears an APRON, and is frying something up on the STOVE. Yoichi stands watching. ASAKAWA Look, Im probably going to be late coming home tonight, so just stick your dinner in the microwave when youre ready to eat, OK? YOICHI K... Mom? ASAKAWA Hmm? Asakawa goes back to the stove, but stops after only a few stirs, staring off and thinking. Caption-- September 13th. Monday. EXT. COUNTRY ROAD DAY Asakawas car drives past a sign reading: IZU PACIFIC LAND EXT. Asakawa lowers the photo to regard the cottage before her. B4 She walks to the door, turns the handle experimentally. Its open. Asakawa walks in. INT. PACIFIC LAND - COTTAGE B4 DAY Asakawa lets her eyes wander around the cottage. It looks very modern, all wood paneling and spacious comfort. Her eyes rest on the TV/VCR setup at the front of the room. Crouching before the VCR now, she presses the eject button. Nothing happens. She fingers the inside of the deck, finds it empty, then reaches behind to the rear of the VCR, searching. Again, there is nothing. Asakawa presses the power button on the television, picks up the REMOTE, and takes a seat on the SOFA. She runs through a few channels but theyre all talk shows, no clues whatsoever. She flicks the TV off and leans back in the sofa, sighing. Just then, she spies a LEDGER on the coffee table. These things are sometimes left in hotels in Japan, so that guests can write a few comments about their stay for others to read. Asakawa picks the ledger up, begins thumbing through it. She stops at a strange PICTURE obviously drawn by a child, that shows three rotund, almost entirely round personages. She reads the handwritten MESSAGE. ASAKAWA "My dad is fat. My mom is fat. Thats why Im fat, too." She smiles in spite of herself. Asakawa flips through the rest of the ledger, but theres nothing else of any import. She tosses it back onto the coffee table and, sighing again, leans into the sofa and closes her eyes. EXT. OUTDOOR CAF - DUSK Asakawa eats silently, alone. INT. PACIFIC LAND - FRONT RECEPTION - NIGHT Asakawa has returned to the bed and breakfast. As she walks in the door, the COUNTER CLERK rises out of his chair to greet her. CLERK Room for one? ASAKAWA They would have stayed here on August 29th, all four of them. If theres any information you might have... CLERK Uh, hang on just a minute. She feels the hairs on the back of her neck rise. ASAKAWA That... The clerk looks up. CLERK Hmm? Asakawa stabs a finger excitedly towards the shelf. ASAKAWA That! What tape is that? The clerk reaches out for it, grabs it. CLERK This? Hmm... The clerk pulls the tape out of its SLEEVE and checks for a label. Its unmarked. CLERK Maybe one of the guests left it behind INT. THE VIDEOTAPE At first it looks like nothing has happened-- then Asakawa realizes that she is now viewing recorded static instead of broadcast static. She watches, waiting, but the static continues unbroken. Asakawa looks down at the remote, is about to press fast forward, when suddenly the picture on the screen clears and for a moment she thinks shes looking at the moon. Its not the moon at all, she realizes. The shape is round like a full moon, but it seems to be made up of thin RIBBONS of cloud streaking against a night sky. And theres a FACE, she sees, a face hidden in shadows, looking down from above. What is this? The scene changes now, and Asakawa notes that the tape has that kind of grainy quality one sees in 3rd or 4th generation copies. The scene is of a WOMAN brushing her long hair before an oval-shaped MIRROR. The nerve- wracking grating as if of some giant metallic insect sounds in the background, but the lady doesnt seem to notice. The mirror the lady is using to brush her hair suddenly changes position from the left part of the wall before which she stands, to the right. Almost instantly the mirror returns to its original position, but in that one moment in its changed location we see a small FIGURE in a white GOWN. The woman turns towards where that figure stood, and smiles. The screen next becomes a twitching, undulating impenetrable sea of the kanji characters used in the Japanese language. Asakawa can pick out only two things recognizable: local volcanic eruption Now the screen is awash in PEOPLE-- crawling, scrabbling, shambling masses, some of them moving in reverse. A sound like moaning accompanies them. - A FIGURE stands upon a shore, its face shrouded. It points accusingly, not towards the screen, but at something unseen off to one side. The insect-like screeching sounds louder. -- Close up on inhuman, alien-looking EYE. Inside that eye a single character is reflected in reverse: SADA, meaning "chastity." The eye blinks once, twice. The symbol remains. --- A long shot of an outdoor, uncovered WELL. ---- Sudden loud, blinding STATIC as the tape ends. Asakawa turns the TV off, looking physically drained. She sighs shakily and slumps forward, resting on her knees. Just then, she glances at the television screen. She sees, reflected, a small FIGURE in a white gown standing at the rear of the room. Shocked, Asakawa draws in breath, spins around. The room is empty. Asakawa runs to the sofa to collect her jacket-- --and the RINGING of the telephone stops her dead in her tracks. Asakawa slams the phone down and glances up at the CLOCK. Its about seven minutes after 7 P.M. So now you're happy.

BILL

What's the matter?

What do you want from me?

BILL

(nods)

ABBY

ABBY

BILL

BILL

(tearfully)

**Justice** is a play by John Galsworthy that explores themes of crime, punishment, and the social structures that perpetuate cycles of despair. The story revolves around William Falder, a young clerk who is driven to commit forgery under emotional duress due to his entanglement with a married woman, Ruth Honeywill, who is trapped in an abusive marriage. The play examines the harshness of the legal system and the long-term consequences of criminal conviction.

### Plot Summary

1. **Act I**: The play opens in the office of solicitors James and Walter How. Falder, a junior clerk, is confronted about a forged cheque. Despite his plea for leniency, he is arrested and taken away, leaving his colleagues in shock.

2. **Act II**: The trial of Falder takes place. His defense team argues that he was temporarily insane due to emotional distress. However, the judge dismisses this plea and sentences him to three years' penal servitude.

3. **Act III**: The play shifts to a prison where Falder is struggling with isolation and despair. The scenes depict the harsh conditions and the psychological toll on prisoners. Falder's mental state deteriorates, culminating in a breakdown.

4. **Act IV**: Two years after his release, Falder, now a shadow of his former self, seeks redemption. He tries to rebuild his life but faces societal stigma and further legal entanglements. The play ends tragically with Falder's rearrest and a suggestion of his eventual decline.

### Themes

- **Injustice and Redemption**: The play critiques the criminal justice system for its rigidity and failure to rehabilitate. Falder's repeated entanglements with the law highlight the cyclical nature of crime and punishment.
- **Social Class and Morality**: The characters' actions are influenced by societal expectations and class constraints. Ruth's inability to escape her marriage and Falder's downfall illustrate the limited options for those trapped by circumstance.
- **Psychological Impact**: The play delves into the mental health of characters, showing how isolation and despair can lead to breakdowns and further criminal behavior.

### Characters

- **William Falder**: The protagonist, a young clerk whose life unravels due to his emotional entanglement and subsequent conviction. His journey from a hopeful clerk to a broken ex-convict is central to the play.
- **Ruth Honeywill**: A woman trapped in an abusive marriage, her relationship with Falder drives much of the plot. Her resilience and ultimate defeat mirror the societal constraints placed on women.
- **James How**: The strict, uncompromising solicitor who represents the legal system's rigidity. His refusal to show leniency underscores the play's critique of justice.
- **Walter How**: James's son, who shows more empathy but ultimately conforms to societal norms, highlighting the internal conflict between compassion and duty.

### Style and Structure

Galsworthy's writing is realistic and nuanced, with a focus on dialogue and psychological depth. The play's structure, divided into four acts, mirrors the progression of Falder's downfall and the inexorable march of justice.

### Conclusion

*Justice* is a powerful critique of a society that fails to rehabilitate its criminals, instead perpetuating cycles of crime through harsh punishments and social stigma. The play's exploration of human frailty and the legal system's shortcomings remains relevant, offering a poignant commentary on the need for compassion and understanding in the administration of justice.

4. **Act IV**: Two years later, Falder is released but struggles to reintegrate. He and Ruth seek help from his former employers, but their past haunts them. The play ends tragically with Falder's apparent death after a fall, emphasizing the irreparable damage caused by the system.

### Style and Structure:

Galsworthy's play uses realistic dialogue and settings to depict the lives of its characters. The structure moves from the legal office to the courtroom and prison, each setting reinforcing the play's themes of entrapment and justice. The play's ending leaves the audience reflecting on the failures of the legal system and the human cost of rigid morality.

**Justice** remains a powerful critique of the legal system, urging empathy and understanding in the application of the law.

She turns, still distant. JACOB's eyes lock on her. He is overcome with emotion. JACOB Mother. The SOLDIERS pull him closer to LOUIS. LOUIS places a gentle hand on JACOB's head. some of my African curiosities. Among other things I showed
him that powder, and I told him of its strange properties, how it was
used in a native ordeal, and how, when it is dropped into the fire,
it is converted into a powerful and instantaneous poison. I told him
that a pinch of it would inflame the passions of the heart and produce
extreme mental excitement. When he left me that day, it is no secret
that he stole a quantity of the powder from the store-room.

Next day he came again, and persuaded me to come out upon the moor and
test the quality of his shooting by firing at a mark--I use the word
"persuaded" because he obtained his end by a little cheating and
deception, for he said that he was attempting a cure upon himself and
desired my company for a longer walk than he could manage alone. As we
walked, his conversation became more and more sinister, and I could
not doubt that, whatever his intention, it was something of which I
would have no reason to be proud. Still I had no idea of the actual
horror which he had in his mind.

"His request, as we walked, was that I would look back at the house and
see if the curtains of his window were open. They were open far more
than is usual with him, so he said. He appeared to be in a state of
great excitement, and he asked me to go back with him. I did so, and
we found that the dogs were loose in the garden. Looking up at his
window as we approached it, I saw the blind was up, and I could have
sworn that someone was standing just behind it, but he assured me it
was merely Brenda, his sister, who was playing a trick upon him. He
entered the house, and the dogs being put away, we proceeded to the
room in which the powder was kept. He had made his plans, I suppose,
for the rest.

"It is nearly incredible to me, after all that I have been through,
that I should have allowed him to deceive me, but he was so subtle, so
skilful, that at no time did I realize his true intentions. The next
thing I remember was that we were walking upon the moor, and he, with
his mischievous grin, was placing the stuff into my hand. He was
laughing, I remember, and saying that it would take me to Africa. I
threw it into the bushes and came straight back to the cottage. But
there was some of the devil's stuff still in my hand, and it got into my
eyes, causing me the most intense pain. When I awoke in the morning I
found that my sight was affected, and from that day I suffered from
vivid dreams and an unaccountable sense of fear. As to the rest, you
know."

There was a silence after the doctor had finished his explanation. The
great detective shook his head in a slow, emphatic negative. "No, Dr.
Sterndale, it is not the end," said he. "The chapter may be closed in
this dramatic and tragic way, but your journey is not yet ended. If I
have heard your statement correctly, and if I follow the course of your
narrative, you leave us in the position of believing that the Tregennis
family was the victim of Mortimer Tregennis, who, in order to win his
sister for some fancied slight, used this devilish poison. Such an idea
is, as you say, incredible, but it is not beyond the bounds of human
ingenuity. But how about the second death? How are we to account for
the fact that the lodger, after a considerable interval, met so
tragical an end?"

"Ah, that is where the true subtlety of the man comes in," said
Sterndale. "He would have made his own escape good by leaving some
suicidal trace which would cover his tracks. But I have to thank you,
Mr. Holmes, for the actual solution of his death. Depression and
remorse have eaten into his mind, and the final scene at the vicarage
must have touched whatever was left of his sanity. He must have
killed himself at the very moment when he realized that the condemnation
of his crime was certain."

"But his sister?"

"Miss Brenda? She died of fright."

"Of fright? No."

"Of heart disease, perhaps?"

"No, the circumstances were as you have heard. She was in her night
clothes, sitting up in her bed. The local practitioner was called in,
and he says the symptoms are those of a paroxysm of fear leading to
apoplexy. So, in short, my dear Mr. Holmes, I leave it to you to
expose such a case. As far as I can see, the chain of events is as
complete as it is tragic. I have no doubt that the temporary madness of
the other two was due to the same cause, and that they would have
recovered from their delirium had the second shock not killed the sister
and driven them out of their senses. Now, I must implore your
discretion for my own sake, for my reason, and even for my life's sake.
If this matter were brought to the ears of the public, there would be an
end to my career, to my liberty, and perhaps to my life."

The great detective arose and struck his forehead with his hand. "I
confess that I am at a loss," said he. "All my efforts to reconstruct
this case have been in vain. I must see the matter more clearly. Where
is the connection between this dead man and the secret of the Cornish
Horror?"

As he spoke, his eyes were fixed upon the little heap of reddish-brown
powder upon the table. A light had suddenly sprung up in them which,
with a quick movement, he quenched by turning away.

"Wait a minute," said he. "I think I need a little more material. No,
it is not material that I need--it is permission."

"Permission?"

"Yes, the permission of Dr. Leon Sterndale to make use of certain
material which is in his possession. Is it there?"

"Yes."

"Then I must have it."

"But how?"

"Without his knowledge?"

"Without his knowledge, if possible."

"But why?"

"Because it is the only way. Mr. Roundhay, we have much to discuss.
The game's afoot, and it must not be lost."

With that he turned upon his heel, and we followed him out of the
arbour. As we went, the great detective's face was set like a mask,
and his eyes gleamed with the intensity of the chase. He had picked up
the trail, and nothing should turn him aside.

It may be that I can never again leave the impressions of this day. My
mind is a jumble of conflicting thoughts and emotions. But I can say
one thing: if the devil himself had to pick a man for his work upon
earth, he would have found him in Dr. Leon Sterndale.

As I write these words, I can feel the creeping chill of fear, and I
know that I can never erase the memory of this day.

some of my African curiosities. Among other things I showed
him that powder, warning him of its deadly efficacy. I say now that I
was a fool to do so, since I knew his nature, but I was off my guard.
He was much interested in it, and asked me some questions about it--I
daresay to satisfy his infamous curiosity. I told him that it was
incredibly deadly, and that the merest grain of it would kill a man in
an instant. At his request I even produced and showed him the actual
root from which the powder is extracted, but I was careful to warn him
that it should on no account be touched. He laughed at my warnings and
persisted in asking why, if it were so deadly, the medicine-men were not
dead who handled it so freely. I told him that while the medicine-men
had an antidote they kept it most jealously, and that none had ever
laid hands upon it but their own priests.

"I remember his words clearly. He said, 'Well, it's all right, for I
have my antidote handy.' It was in that very moment, I believe, that
he conceived the idea of using the poison. I next saw him on the night
of the tragedy, and for some time I was inclined to suspect that he had
the poison with him in the paper packet which he held in his hand. That
must have been the time when he threw it into the fire. The devil knows
the way he used it that night, but I think that all that is in the
future."

With these words the African explorer folded his arms upon his breast,
and the mystery which had puzzled even the greatest of detectives for
its solution was laid bare.

It was on the 3rd of May that we heard the Premier announce in the
House of Commons the great discovery which had been made in the
South-West of England, and three days later the country rang with the
horrible details of the Dartmoor Tragedy. Early on the morning of the
2nd of May three Huluvu natives, as they are called, had been found
dead, their bodies horribly mutilated, upon the moor. When the
inquest was held a man named John Stanley, a convict who had served a
sentence for murder, was arrested and charged with the crime.

The evidence against him was of the most convincing character, and it
is now certain that he was guilty. But the story of the crime is one
which might well have happened in darkest Africa rather than in the very
heart of our English counties. The three men had been found with their
faces contorted into the most horrible grimaces, their eyes turned
upwards, and their bodies rigid. The first man had his throat
severely lacerated, the second had a deep wound in the face, the third
had been disembowelled. The weapon used was a curved knife of native
workmanship. It is the opinion of the authorities that the man Stanley
had in some way come into contact with the three Huluvus before the
murder, had probably some strong grudge against them, and had killed
them in this particularly atrocious manner as a result of his hatred.

But the interest which was excited by this horrible crime was as nothing
to that which was caused by the discovery which followed. The bodies of
the three men had been found by a party of miners at a spot not far
from the scene of the Tregennis tragedy. On the same spot there was
found a fourth body, that of Dr. Leon Sterndale, the well-known African
explorer. He had apparently died as he fell, for there were no marks of
a struggle, but the flesh of his face was horribly drawn and distorted,
and his eyes turned upwards and fixed. The medical evidence at the
inquest was to the effect that his death was due to an affection of the
heart induced by the horror of the scene before him. It was evident
that he had died when he caught sight of the mutilated bodies of the
Huluvu men.

The proceedings at the inquest upon the four bodies were very
sensational, and the evidence of the miners was to the effect that the
Huluvus had been found with the same look of frozen horror on their
faces as was observed upon the features of Dr. Sterndale. It was
clear that in some way the African explorer had been directly connected
with the Huluvus, and that some terrible vengeance had been taken upon
him for some action which he had committed against them during his stay
in their native land.

The story of the Dartmoor Horror, as it will ever be known, is one
which many will remember for many years to come, and it is a story of
which the curious details will probably never be fully and
satisfactorily explained. It is a story of how a great and daring
man, who had faced uncounted perils in his adventures, met his own
death under circumstances which were as tragic as they were strange, and
of how the avenging spirits of the distant jungle, the "devils" as we
might call them, followed him even to the quiet English countryside and
struck him down in the very heart of his own home.

*Setting:* The raised porch of Joe Clark's store and the street in front. The villagers are gathered on the porch, socializing and conducting their Saturday afternoon activities. The scene opens with the villagers chewing sugar cane and discussing various topics.

*Daisy Taylor* arrives, and the conversation shifts to her popularity and the rivalry between *Jim* and *Dave* over her affections. The two men argue, and their friends try to mediate. *Jim* and *Dave* perform music and dance, but their rivalry escalates into a fight when *Jim* strikes *Dave* with the mule bone.

The villagers gather at the church, and *Dr. Leon Sterndale* arrives, revealing his connection to the Tregennis family and the source of the poison used in the tragedy. *Holmes* investigates and deduces that *Mortimer* was involved in the death of his family and his own demise.

The story "The Coxon Fund" by Henry James revolves around the complex relationships and moral dilemmas faced by several characters, particularly George Gravener and Ruth Anvoy, as they navigate the intricacies of love, ambition, and the influence of a substantial sum of money known as The Coxon Fund. The narrative delves into themes of greed, morality, and the consequences of one's actions, set against the backdrop of societal expectations and personal aspirations.

### Key Themes:
1. **Moral Ambiguity and Compromise**: The story explores the gray areas between right and wrong, particularly through George Gravener's willingness to support Frank Saltram for The Coxon Fund, despite moral reservations. This highlights the tension between personal ambition and ethical integrity.

2. **Influence of Wealth**: The Coxon Fund serves as a catalyst for the characters' actions, illustrating how the promise of money can manipulate decisions and relationships. Lady Coxon's obsession with the fund and her desire to use it for her own interpretation of "Moral Truth" drive much of the plot.

3. **Love and Sacrifice**: Ruth Anvoy's engagement to George Gravener is tested by her family's financial crisis and her own sense of duty. Her decision to help her father while maintaining her commitment to Gravener shows the complexity of love and sacrifice.

4. **Deception and Secrecy**: The story is rife with hidden agendas and unspoken truths, particularly Gravener's secret plan to secure The Coxon Fund for Frank Saltram, which threatens to undermine his relationship with Ruth.

### Character Analysis:
- **George Gravener**: A pragmatic and ambitious politician, Gravener is torn between his duty to his fiancée and the allure of advancing his career through The Coxon Fund. His internal conflict reflects the struggle between personal integrity and public image.

- **Ruth Anvoy**: An idealistic and generous young woman, Ruth is caught between her loyalty to her family and her love for Gravener. Her character embodies the tension between moral idealism and practical realities.

- **Frank Saltram**: A charismatic but flawed intellectual, Saltram represents the allure of genius and the pitfalls of moral laxity. His influence over others highlights the power of personality and ideas.

- **Lady Coxon**: A dying woman obsessed with her late husband's vision of The Coxon Fund, Lady Coxon's actions are driven by a misguided sense of duty and a desire to leave a legacy, leading to manipulative and destructive behavior.

### Climax:
The story reaches its climax when Gravener reveals that Lady Coxon intends to marry Frank Saltram to secure The Coxon Fund for him. This revelation exposes the depth of Lady Coxon's obsession and the moral compromise Gravener is willing to make. The climax underscores the destructive potential of unchecked ambition and the blurred lines between right and wrong.

### Conclusion:
The narrative leaves the reader with a sense of foreboding and unease, as the characters' decisions set in motion a chain of events that will have far-reaching consequences. The story serves as a cautionary tale about the dangers of allowing ambition and greed to overshadow moral principles, and the delicate balance between personal and public responsibilities.

Fougeres opened his mouth to speak, but no words came.

"Vervelle," said Magus. "You can paint her, but can you marry her?"

"Ah, I see you are ready."

"Wait," said Fougeres. "I must think."

"If you are going to think," said Magus, "let me think."

Magus took his way out of the studio, leaving Fougeres in a state of
extreme perturbation. He had never thought that Elie's suggestion would
lead him to a marriage.

Fougeres' studio was in the rue de Navarin, and he went to his bed,

up his mind to the thought of marrying a girl for her dot, but he could
not either make up his mind to giving up the match.

The next day, Fougeres was in a state of fever. He went to see Magus,

would be settled.

Fougeres was in a state of distraction. He thought of the dowry and
the titles, and saw before him a future of happiness and success. He
imagined himself as a great artist, with a wife who was a true artist,
a wife who would not only manage his household, but who would also be
his partner in his artistic work. He thought of her as a woman who
understood the arts, and who would be of assistance to him in his
ambitions.

At the same time, he thought of the family who had given their consent.
They were good people, retired from business, who had made their
fortune in the bottle trade. He thought of their respectability and
their reputation, and saw in them a connection which would be of
advantage to him.

Fougeres made up his mind, and on the same day he married Mademoiselle
Vervelle. The marriage was a happy one, and the two were married in
the presence of their friends and family.

But as time passed, Fougeres began to realize that he had made a mistake.
His wife was not the woman he had imagined. She was not the artist's
wife, but a bourgeoise, who had no understanding of his art. She
managed the household, but she did not assist him in his work. She was
cold, and showed no interest in his ambitions.

Fougeres' disappointment was great, and he began to regret his
marriage. He had thought that he would find happiness and success, but
he found instead a life of misery and failure. His art suffered, and he
became a forgotten man in the artistic circles. He realized that he had
married for money, and that he had lost his true love for art.

In the end, Fougeres was left alone, his marriage a failure, his art
forgotten, and his life a disappointment. He died in obscurity, a
mediocrity who had never achieved his true potential.

Thus, the story of Pierre Grassou serves as a cautionary tale of the

**The Ring: A Story of Cursed Videotapes and Supernatural Horrors**

**Introduction:**

The screenplay adaptation of Suzuki Koji's novel *Ring* presents a chilling tale of a cursed videotape that leads to the deaths of those who watch it within a week. The story intertwines elements of mystery, supernatural horror, and psychological tension, keeping viewers on the edge of their seats.

**Plot Summary:**

The story begins with two high school girls, Masami and Tomoko, discussing an urban legend about a cursed videotape. Tomoko reveals that she watched a strange video with her friends, and exactly one week later, she receives a mysterious phone call, leading to her death. As the story unfolds, a journalist named Reiko Asakawa investigates the mystery of the cursed tape, discovering that it is linked to a tragic event involving a woman named Sadako, who was wrongfully killed and thrown into a well. The curse is perpetuated as each viewer of the tape dies exactly one week later, unless they can uncover the truth and break the cycle.

**Key Themes:**

1. **Urban Legends and Supernatural Elements:** The cursed videotape serves as a vehicle for the vengeful spirit of Sadako, creating a bridge between urban legend and supernatural horror.

2. **Psychological Tension and Fear:** The story builds suspense through the countdown to the characters' deaths, emphasizing the psychological impact of fear and the unknown.

3. **Family Secrets and Tragedy:** The backstory of Sadako and her father, Professor Ikuma, reveals a dark history of betrayal and murder, providing depth to the curse's origins.

4. **Investigation and Resolution:** Reiko Asakawa's relentless pursuit of the truth showcases determination and the human need to uncover hidden secrets, even in the face of danger.

**Conclusion:**

The screenplay masterfully weaves together elements of horror, mystery, and psychological drama, creating a narrative that captivates audiences. The curse of the videotape serves as a metaphor for the enduring impact of unresolved tragedies and the consequences of delving into the unknown. Through its intricate plot and chilling climax, *The Ring* leaves a lasting impression, reminding viewers of the power of stories to both entertain and terrify.

**Mary: A Fiction** by Mary Wollstonecraft is a novel that delves into the life of its protagonist, Mary, exploring themes of love, loss, and the societal constraints placed on women during the late 18th century. The story follows Mary's journey through her formative years, her marriage, and her deep emotional connections, ultimately leading to her tragic demise.

1. **Mary's Early Life**: The novel begins with Mary's childhood, highlighting her sensitive nature and intellectual curiosity. Her parents' neglect and lack of affection contribute to her emotional struggles, but she finds solace in nature, reading, and her friendship with Ann.

2. **Marriage and Motherhood**: Mary is forced into a marriage with Charles, a union that brings her neither happiness nor fulfillment. Her role as a mother is overshadowed by her own health issues and the death of her children, further isolating her.

3. **Friendship and Love**: The narrative emphasizes Mary's deep and often unrequited friendships, particularly with Ann. Her friendship with Henry, whom she meets in Lisbon, evolves into a romantic connection, offering her moments of happiness amidst her sorrow.

4. **Themes of Mortality and Suffering**: The novel explores themes of death and suffering, with Mary experiencing the loss of multiple loved ones, including her mother, friend Ann, and ultimately Henry. These losses profoundly affect her mental and physical health.

5. **Social Commentary**: Wollstonecraft critiques the societal norms of her time, particularly the limited roles and opportunities available to women. Mary's struggle for independence and her desire to break free from societal expectations are central to the narrative.

6. **Psychological Insight**: The novel provides a deep psychological portrayal of Mary, showcasing her internal conflicts, emotional vulnerability, and resilience. Her struggles with depression, anxiety, and the pressures of societal expectations are vividly depicted.

7. **Tragic Conclusion**: The novel concludes with Mary's death, a consequence of her prolonged emotional and physical suffering. Her burial alongside Henry symbolizes the enduring nature of their love and her ultimate escape from the hardships of her life.

**Mary: A Fiction** is a poignant exploration of the human condition, emphasizing the struggles faced by women in a society governed by rigid norms and expectations. It remains a significant work in the literary canon, offering insights into the life and philosophy of Mary Wollstonecraft, a pioneering figure in feminist thought.

Mary is a tragic tale that follows the life of its titular character, Mary, a deeply sensitive and emotional woman living in the late 18th century. The novel explores themes of love, loss, and the societal constraints placed on women, highlighting the devastating consequences of unchecked sensibility and the rigid social norms of the time.

**Plot Summary:**

Mary is born into a family where her parents are largely indifferent to her emotional needs. Her father is tyrannical and passion-driven, while her mother is vain and more concerned with social appearances than her children's well-being. Mary grows up in a neglectful environment, finding solace in nature, books, and her own imagination.

As she matures, Mary becomes deeply attached to her friend Ann, who is equally troubled by her own circumstances. The two form a close bond, but their relationship is marked by unrequited emotions and disappointment. Ann's health declines, and Mary dedicates herself to caring for her, even as she faces her own marital obligations. Mary is forced into a loveless marriage, which she deeply resents, and she finds herself increasingly isolated.

When Ann dies, Mary is consumed by grief and throws herself into acts of benevolence to alleviate her pain. She travels to Lisbon with Ann's body, where she meets Henry, a kind and intellectual man who becomes the object of her affection. Henry, however, is terminally ill, and their relationship is doomed from the start.

The novel reaches its tragic conclusion as Henry dies, leaving Mary heartbroken and spiraling into madness and despair. Her mental and physical health deteriorate rapidly, and she eventually dies, a victim of her own sensibility and the harsh realities of her world.

**Themes:**

1. **Sensibility and Emotion:** The novel explores the double-edged nature of extreme emotional sensitivity. While it allows Mary to experience deep connections and empathy, it also leads to her downfall as she is overwhelmed by grief and loss.

2. **Social Constraints:** Mary's life is heavily influenced by the societal norms of her time, particularly the limited options available to women. Her forced marriage and the lack of support for her intellectual pursuits highlight the oppressive nature of her environment.

3. **Love and Loss:** The novel is a poignant exploration of unrequited and doomed love. Mary's relationships with Ann and Henry are central to the story, and their tragic endings underscore the cruel fate that awaits her.

4. **Religion and Spirituality:** Mary's spiritual journey and her devotion to a higher power serve as both a source of comfort and a means of coping with her suffering. Her religious convictions provide a framework for understanding her trials but ultimately fail to save her from despair.

5. **Mental Health:** The novel portrays the devastating impact of grief and loss on mental health. Mary's descent into madness and her eventual death serve as a cautionary tale about the fragility of the human psyche.

**Style and Structure:**

The novel is written in a reflective and philosophical style, with Mary's internal monologues and emotional struggles taking center stage. Wollstonecraft's prose is lyrical and expressive, capturing the intense emotions and intellectual depth of her protagonist. The structure is episodic, with each chapter focusing on key events and emotional turning points in Mary's life.

**Cultural and Historical Context:**

Written in the late 18th century, *Mary* reflects the societal attitudes and challenges faced by women during this period. The novel is a product of the Age of Sensibility, a literary movement that emphasized emotional depth and individualism. Wollstonecraft's work critiques the social conventions that trapped women in loveless marriages and limited their intellectual and emotional expression.

**Reception and Legacy:**

*Mary* was not widely recognized during Wollstonecraft's lifetime but has since been acknowledged as a significant work in the feminist literary tradition. It is celebrated for its exploration of female experience and its critique of patriarchal society. The novel's tragic tone and emotional depth have influenced later writers exploring similar themes of love, loss, and female identity.

**Conclusion:**

*Mary* is a powerful and poignant exploration of a woman's struggle against the constraints of her society and the overwhelming power of her own emotions. Through Mary's tragic journey, Wollstonecraft sheds light on the vulnerabilities and strengths of the female experience, leaving behind a timeless tale of love, loss, and resilience.

**Mary, A Fiction** by Mary Wollstonecraft is a deeply emotional and philosophical novel that explores the life of its titular character, Mary, as she navigates through the challenges of love, loss, and societal expectations. The story is structured into thirty chapters, each delving into various aspects of Mary's inner world and her interactions with the people around her.

### Plot Summary:

**Chapters I-VI: Early Life and Marriage**

Mary's early life is marked by a troubled home environment. Her parents are indifferent to her, and she finds solace in nature and books. Her father, Edward, forces her into a marriage with Charles, a man she does not love, to secure the family's financial interests. Mary's mother dies shortly after the wedding, leaving her feeling isolated and trapped in a loveless marriage.

**Chapters VII-XII: Friendship and Loss**

Mary forms a deep friendship with Ann, a woman from a poor background. Ann's health deteriorates, and Mary dedicates herself to caring for her. Despite their close bond, Ann's death leaves Mary devastated. During this time, Mary also faces the death of her father and the emotional turmoil of her failing marriage.

**Chapters XIII-XXIII: Lisbon and Henry**

Seeking a change of scenery and hoping to escape her husband, Mary travels to Lisbon with Ann. There, she meets Henry, a kind and intellectual man who shares her love for literature and music. Henry's ill health and their deepening bond create a complex emotional dynamic. Mary finds herself torn between her duty to her husband and her growing feelings for Henry.

**Chapters XXIV-XXX: Tragic Conclusion**

Henry's health declines further, and Mary nurses him until his death. His passing leaves Mary in a state of profound grief. She returns to England and reunites with her husband, Charles, but their relationship remains strained. The novel ends with Mary fainting in her bedroom, overwhelmed by the cumulative pain of her losses.

### Themes:

1. **Feminism and Independence**: Mary's struggle for autonomy in a society that restricts women's choices is a central theme. Her desire to live apart from her husband and pursue her own path reflects the feminist ideals Wollstonecraft is known for.

2. **Love and Loss**: The novel explores the intensity of love and the devastating impact of loss. Mary's relationships with Ann and Henry are portrayed as deeply emotional and transformative.

3. **Religion and Philosophy**: Mary's internal conflicts and philosophical musings about life, death, and spirituality are woven throughout the narrative. Her faith and search for meaning add depth to her character.

4. **Societal Critique**: Wollstonecraft critiques the social norms and class structures of her time, particularly the treatment of women and the poor. Mary's interactions with various characters highlight these issues.

### Character Analysis:

- **Mary**: The protagonist is a sensitive, intelligent, and deeply emotional woman. Her strength lies in her resilience and her capacity for love, but she is also vulnerable to the societal pressures and personal tragedies that surround her.

- **Henry**: Henry represents the ideal of a kind, intellectual, and emotionally available partner. His death serves as a catalyst for Mary's emotional breakdown.

- **Ann**: Ann is a symbol of female friendship and solidarity. Her illness and death underscore the fragility of life and the depth of Mary's emotional connections.

- **Charles**: Charles embodies the societal expectations placed on women. His character highlights the limitations of arranged marriages and the lack of emotional fulfillment they often bring.

### Style and Structure:

The novel is written in a lyrical and introspective style, with a focus on Mary's inner thoughts and emotions. The use of nature as a backdrop for her emotional states is a recurring motif, symbolizing both her connection to the sublime and her internal turmoil. The structure, divided into short chapters, allows for a detailed exploration of Mary's psyche and the progression of her story.

### Conclusion:

"Mary, A Fiction" is a poignant exploration of a woman's struggle to find her place in a world that often seems hostile to her desires and needs. Through Mary's journey, Wollstonecraft delivers a powerful critique of societal norms and a deeply human story of love, loss, and resilience. The novel remains a significant work in the canon of feminist literature, offering insights into the complexities of the female experience in the late 18th century.

**The Adventure of the Devil's Foot**

By Sir Arthur Conan Doyle

In this intriguing story, Sherlock Holmes is faced with a peculiar and tragic case involving the Tregennis family. The family is found in a state of horror, with one member dead and the others driven to madness. Holmes must uncover the cause of this terrifying event and bring the perpetrator to justice.

1. **Initial Setup**: Holmes and Dr. Watson are in a small cottage in Cornwall, where they meet with Mr. Mortimer Tregennis and the vicar, Mr. Roundhay. They learn of the family's tragic fate and the strange circumstances surrounding it.

2. **The Mystery Unfolds**: The family was found with expressions of extreme horror, and there is no apparent cause or intruder. Holmes begins his investigation by examining the house and interviewing those involved.

3. **Theories and Clues**: Holmes considers various possibilities, including supernatural elements, but focuses on finding a natural explanation. He discovers that the family was exposed to a toxic substance, likely inhaled from a lamp or fire.

4. **The Perpetrator**: Holmes deduces that Mortimer Tregennis was responsible for the tragedy. He had used a rare poison called "Devil's-foot root" to incapacitate his family, driven by a twisted sense of revenge and guilt.

5. **The Aftermath**: Holmes confronts Dr. Leon Sterndale, a friend of the family, who reveals that he was involved in the case due to his love for Brenda Tregennis. Sterndale admits to helping Mortimer Tregennis escape but later kills him in a fit of revenge.

6. **Conclusion**: Holmes decides not to expose Sterndale, recognizing the moral complexity of the situation. The case highlights the darker aspects of human nature and the consequences of unchecked emotions.

**Crito**

By Plato

This philosophical dialogue explores the ethical dilemma faced by Socrates as he considers escaping from prison. The main arguments revolve around the conflict between individual conscience and societal law.

1. **Setting**: Socrates is in prison, awaiting execution. His friend Crito visits him and urges him to escape, citing the potential consequences for his friends and family.

2. **Moral Debate**: Socrates engages in a deep discussion with Crito about justice, morality, and the role of the state. He argues that escaping would be unjust, as he has implicitly agreed to abide by the state's laws.

3. **The Law's Perspective**: Socrates personifies the laws of Athens, which argue that he has a duty to accept the state's decisions, including his death sentence, as he has benefited from them throughout his life.

4. **Conclusion**: Socrates concludes that escaping would be wrong and decides to accept his fate. The dialogue emphasizes the importance of adhering to justice and the rule of law, even in the face of death.

**Justice**

By John Galsworthy

This play explores the British legal system and its impact on individuals, focusing on the case of William Falder, who is convicted of forgery.

1. **Act I**: The story begins in a solicitor's office where Falder is accused of altering a cheque. His personal life, involving a woman named Ruth Honeywill, complicates the situation.

2. **Act II**: The trial takes place, and Falder is found guilty. The defense argues for temporary insanity due to emotional distress, but the court sentences him to five years' penal servitude.

3. **Act III**: Falder's time in prison leads to his psychological deterioration. He faces further distress upon learning that Ruth may not be the person he believed her to be.

4. **Act IV**: The play concludes with Falder's death in prison, highlighting the harsh consequences of the legal system and the personal tragedies involved.

Each of these works delves into themes of morality, justice, and the human condition, providing profound insights into the complexities of ethical decision-making and societal structures.

**Armageddon—2419 A.D.**

By Philip Francis Nowlan

**Foreword**

In the year 2419, Anthony Rogers, a man from the 20th century, awakens from a 492-year-long hibernation to find the world drastically changed. The United States has been conquered by the Hans, a Mongolian empire, and Americans are a hunted race living in the forests. The story follows Rogers as he joins the Wyoming Gang, a group of rebels fighting against the Hans, and becomes a key figure in their struggle for independence.

**Chapter I: Floating Men**

Rogers encounters a young woman named Wilma Deering, who is part of the Wyoming Gang. He learns about the society of the 25th century, including the use of inertron belts that allow people to jump long distances and the structure of the gangs. Rogers and Wilma form a bond as they fight off attackers and navigate the dangers of their new world.

**Chapter II: The Forest Gangs**

Wilma explains the history of the world since Rogers' time, detailing the rise and fall of empires, the development of new technologies, and the formation of the gangs. The Wyoming Gang is a tightly knit community with a mix of military and industrial roles, preparing for a future uprising against the Hans.

**Chapter III: Life in the 25th Century**

Rogers integrates into the Wyoming Gang, learning about their technology, society, and daily life. He visits various plants and meets key figures, including Bill Hearn, a Camp Boss, and Big Boss Hart. Rogers begins to grasp the complexities of the new world and his role within it.

**Chapter IV: A Han Air Raid**

A Han airship attacks the Wyoming Valley, prompting Rogers and Wilma to take action. Rogers uses his knowledge of 20th-century tactics to bring down the ship, demonstrating the effectiveness of his ideas to the gang. The Hans, however, are likely to retaliate, setting the stage for further conflict.

**Chapter V: Setting the Trap**

The Wyoming Gang plans to destroy a Han fleet using Rogers' strategy of targeting the repellor rays. They set up an ambush and successfully destroy the ships, dealing a significant blow to the Hans. This victory boosts the gang's morale and solidifies Rogers' position as a leader.

**Chapter VI: The "Wyoming Massacre"**

The Hans launch a counterattack, but Rogers and the gang are prepared. Using their knowledge of the Han technology and tactics, they annihilate the fleet. The victory is a turning point, showing the Hans that the Americans are a force to be reckoned with.

**Chapter VII: Incredible Treason**

The gang discovers that a traitorous group, the Sinsings, has been providing information to the Hans. Rogers leads a mission to gather evidence and confront the traitors, ensuring their destruction to protect the gang's secrets.

**Chapter VIII: The Han City**

Rogers and a team infiltrate a Han city to gather crucial information. They face dangers and challenges but manage to escape with vital records, furthering their cause against the Hans.

**Chapter IX: The Fight in the Tower**

During the infiltration, the team encounters Han forces, leading to a fierce battle. They successfully complete their mission, but not without close calls and harrowing escapes.

**Chapter X: The Walls of Hell**

The team faces a Han disintegrator wall, a formidable defense system. They narrowly escape destruction through skill and luck, returning as heroes to their gang.

**Chapter XI: The New Boss**

Rogers is appointed the leader of an expedition to destroy the traitorous Sinsings. His leadership and strategic thinking prove crucial in the success of the mission, solidifying his role as a key figure in the fight against the Hans.

**Conclusion**

Rogers' story becomes a historical account of the struggle for independence and the eventual triumph of the Americans over the Hans. His journey from a man out of time to a leader in a new world underscores the resilience and ingenuity of humanity in the face of overwhelming odds.

These days that followed were ones of the most terrible strain. The Bad
Bloods were a treacherous foe, and my company had to fight its way

near the ancient city of Camden. It was a hideous place, with rank

had scouts and spies everywhere.

It was a confused and gory battle in the tangled underbrush. I remember
the snarl of a rocket gun, the explosion of shells, and the final
charge that broke the Bad Bloods and sent them fleeing in panic. We
slaughtered them without quarter, for that was the only way to make the
lesson stick.

But when it was all over, I was left with only sixty-eight of my original
hundred men. The Bad Bloods were exterminated, but it was a costly
victory.

I rejoined the main body just in time to participate in the final stages
of the attack on the Sinsings. It was a larger and more cunning gang
than the Bad Bloods, but by this time our warriors were in a fighting
fury that could not be contained.

We found their camp on the Hudson, a veritable fortress of log and
metal, surrounded by a maze of traps and guards. But the Wyomings were
undeterred, and with a series of lightning raids and clever
maneuvering, we broke through their defenses and put the entire gang to
the sword. The Sinsings were traitors, and they died without mercy.

With both the Bad Bloods and Sinsings exterminated, the Wyoming Gang had
eliminated the most dangerous threats to their security, and had
demonstrated their power and unity to the other American gangs. It was a
turning point in our struggle against the Hans, for now we could focus
all our efforts on the common enemy.

The following months were filled with relentless attacks on the Hans and
their airships. We developed new tactics and strategies, combining the
use of our inertron belts and rocket guns with clever ambushes and
raids. The Hans were caught off guard by our sudden increase in
effectiveness, and their losses mounted steadily.

But the Hans were not easily defeated. They retaliated with fierce
counterattacks, and their disintegrator rays laid waste to many of our
camps and plants. Yet, the Wyomings and their allies were a resilient
people, and they rebuilt and adapted, always pushing forward with
determination and courage.

In the end, it was not just the military might of the Hans that we had
to overcome, but also the internal strife and corruption that threatened
to undermine our own society. As the years passed, the temptation of
power and wealth began to corrupt some of our leaders, and the once-united
gangs started to fragment and fight among themselves.

But through it all, the memory of our struggle against the Hans kept us
united, and the flame of independence burned brightly in our hearts. We
knew that as long as we stood together, there was hope for a future
where America would be free from the yoke of the Mongolian oppressors.

And so, the Second War of Independence continued, a testament to the
strength and resilience of the American spirit, even in the darkest of
times. The road ahead would be long and fraught with peril, but with
unwavering resolve and the support of our people, the Wyomings and their
allies pressed on, determined to reclaim their homeland and forge a new
era of peace and prosperity.

The end of this chapter in our history was but the beginning of another,
as we looked to the future with hope and defiance, ready to face whatever
challenges lay ahead, side by side, as a united and indomitable people.
